title: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) Under the Hood: How Patch Projection and Multimodal Projectors Bridge Pixels and LLMs
summary: Large language models understand the world through discrete token IDs mapped to dense dimensional vectors. Raw image files, by contrast, are continuous grids of pixel brightness values across red, green, and blue color channels. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like LLaVA, GPT-4o, and Gemini bridge this sensory divide without building new model architectures from scratch. By slicing images into 2D patches, encoding spatial features with a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT or SigLIP), and transforming visual embeddings into the LLM's native token embedding space via lightweight multimodal projection layers, modern systems treat visual patches identically to textual words, unlocking unified multimodal reasoning.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Mandarin Technical Manual and The Fast Translation Liaison
analogy:
Imagine a brilliant legal scholar who only speaks English receiving a page from a Mandarin engineering manual containing diagrams and blueprints.

Under an Attempt to Force Raw Data (Direct Pixel Feeding), someone reads the raw ASCII byte codes of the JPEG file aloud to the scholar: '0xFF, 0xD8, 0xFF, 0xE0'. The scholar becomes completely disoriented by meaningless numerical noise.

Under The Modern VLM Architecture (The Patch Interpreter and Projection Liaison), an art archivist first cuts the blueprint page into a 14x14 grid of small square tiles (Patch Projection). The archivist examines each tile's lines, gradients, and textures with a magnifying glass (Vision Transformer). Then, a bilingual liaison translates those visual descriptors into standardized English legal terminology that matches the scholar's vocabulary (The Multimodal Projection Layer). The scholar simply receives a sequence of descriptive concepts right alongside the user's question, understanding the visual layout effortlessly.

sections.heading: 1. From Pixels to Patches: How Vision Transformers Slice the World
sections.content:
Feeding raw pixel values directly into transformer attention layers is mathematically intractable. A standard $1024 \times 1024$ image has over 3 million subpixel values; self-attention across 3 million inputs would require trillions of operations for a single image.

• Patch Tokenization: Vision Transformers (ViT) solve this by slicing an image $I \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ into a grid of non-overlapping 2D patches of size $P \times P$ (typically $14 \times 14$ or $16 \times 16$). A $336 \times 336$ image yields exactly $(336/14) \times (336/14) = 24 \times 24 = 576$ visual patches.
• Linear Patch Projection: Each flattened patch of $14 \times 14 \times 3 = 588$ pixel values is multiplied by a learned linear projection matrix $W_{patch}$ to produce a vector of dimension $d_{vision}$ (e.g., 1024). 2D positional embeddings are added so the network retains horizontal and vertical spatial geometry.

sections.heading: 2. The Multimodal Connector: Aligning Latent Dimensional Spaces
sections.content:
Even after encoding, visual patch vectors cannot be handed directly to an LLM because their dimensional spaces and semantic representations are incompatible ($d_{vision} \neq d_{text}$):

• MLP Projectors (The LLaVA Approach): Popularized by LLaVA (Large Language and Vision Assistant), modern open VLMs use a 2-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with GELU activation functions. The projector maps the 576 visual vectors from $d_{vision}$ (e.g., 1024) into the LLM's token embedding dimension $d_{llm}$ (e.g., 4096).
• Cross-Attention vs. Prefix Concatenation: Older architectures (like DeepMind's Flamingo) used gated cross-attention layers inserted between frozen LLM blocks. Modern architectures favor prefix concatenation: visual tokens are simply prepended to the prompt token sequence: [BOS, <image_patch_1>, ..., <image_patch_576>, 'What', 'is', 'in', 'this', 'photo?', EOS].
• Spatial Compression: To prevent 576 visual tokens from consuming excessive context window memory, architectures use $2 \times 2$ pixel shuffles or spatial pooling, compressing 4 adjacent patches into 1 visual token.

sections.heading: 3. The Two-Stage Training Recipe: Alignment to Instruction Tuning
sections.content:
Training a production Vision-Language Model involves a disciplined two-stage curriculum:

• Stage 1: Pre-training for Feature Alignment: The pre-trained Vision Encoder (SigLIP/CLIP) and the base LLM are frozen. Only the lightweight MLP projector is trained on millions of simple image-caption pairs (e.g., CC3M). The projector learns the dictionary translation from visual features into the text embedding manifold.
• Stage 2: Visual Instruction Tuning: The projector and the LLM weights are unfrozen while the Vision Encoder remains frozen. The model is fine-tuned on diverse conversational data, visual question answering (VQA), chart reading, and coordinate bounding-box grounding. The LLM learns to reason over visual tokens with the same syntactic fluencies as human text.

takeaway: Vision-Language Models do not reinvent transformer mechanics; they treat visual data as pseudo-text tokens. By dividing images into discrete 2D patches with Vision Transformers and mapping visual feature vectors into the LLM's native embedding space via trained projection layers, models can reason across pixels and text with a single unified decoder.
